name: 1 Corinthians
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The earliest substantial manuscript of the letter is P46 (Chester Beatty papyrus, usually dated about AD 200); its readings, like those of other manuscripts, are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Notable textual questions include 13:3 (“so that I may boast” or “to be burned”), the position of 14:34–35 (placed after 14:40 in some Western witnesses), and the wording of 15:51; see the notes there. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from Paul’s Greek, with the source given in a note. Greek *Christos* is rendered “Christ,” as part of Jesus’ name. Greek *adelphoi*, “brothers,” addresses the whole congregation, women and men. Phrases set in quotation marks within Paul’s argument (for example 6:12–13; 7:1; 8:1, 4) are widely taken to be slogans or statements from the Corinthians’ side, though the punctuation is an editorial judgment. The letter is undisputedly Paul’s, sent in the name of Paul and Sosthenes (1:1) from Ephesus (16:8), probably about AD 53–55, in reply to reports and to a letter from Corinth (1:11; 7:1). It refers to an earlier letter that has not survived (5:9).

verses.text: From Paul, called by God’s will to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and from Sosthenes{a} our brother,

to the church of God that is in Corinth,{b} to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:
grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I give thanks to my God at all times on your account, for the grace of God granted you in Christ Jesus;
for in him you were made rich in every way, in all speech and all knowledge,
just as the testimony about Christ was made firm among you,
so that you lack no gift of grace as you eagerly await the unveiling of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He will keep you steady to the very end, beyond reproach on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.{c}
Faithful is God, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Brothers, I appeal to you by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that you all speak with one voice, and that there be no splits among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.
For it has been made known to me about you, my brothers, by Chloe’s{d} people, that there are quarrels among you.
What I mean is this: each of you says, “I belong to Paul,” or “I to Apollos,”{e} or “I to Cephas,”{f} or “I to Christ.”
Has Christ been parceled out? Was Paul crucified on your behalf? Or were you baptized into Paul’s name?
I am thankful{g} that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,
so no one can say that you were baptized into my name.
(I did baptize the household of Stephanas{h} too; beyond that, I do not recall baptizing anyone else.)
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with cleverness of speech, so that the cross of Christ would not be drained of its power.
For the message{i} of the cross is foolishness to those on the way to destruction, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the shrewdness of the shrewd I will set aside.”{j}
Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made foolish the wisdom of the world?
For since, in God’s wisdom, the world did not come to know God through its wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of the message proclaimed to save those who believe.
Jews ask for signs and Greeks look for wisdom,
but we proclaim Christ crucified, an offense to Jews and folly to Gentiles,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
For God’s folly is wiser than human beings, and God’s weakness is stronger than human beings.
Just look at your own calling, brothers: not many of you were wise by worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth.
But God chose what is foolish in the world to put the wise to shame; God chose what is weak in the world to put the strong to shame;
God chose what is lowborn in the world and what is despised, things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,
so that no human being might boast before God.
It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,
so that it may be as Scripture says: “Whoever boasts, let him make his boast in the Lord.”{k}

notes.text: Sosthenes: Greek, “safe in strength”; perhaps the synagogue ruler of Acts 18:17.
Corinth: a Roman colony and capital of the province of Achaia, on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese.
Jesus Christ: “Christ” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Chloe: Greek, “green shoot,” a name of the goddess Demeter.
Apollos: a short form of *Apollonius*, from the god Apollo; a Jewish Christian teacher from Alexandria (Acts 18:24–28).
Cephas: Aramaic *Kepha*, “rock,” rendered in Greek as *Petros*, Peter (John 1:42).
I am thankful: so the Westcott–Hort text with Sinaiticus (original hand) and Vaticanus (as reported); most manuscripts read “I thank God.”
Stephanas: Greek, “crown.”
Message: Greek *logos*, “word.”
Isa 29:14, following the Greek Old Testament.
Jer 9:24. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.

verses.text: For my part, brothers, when I came to you, I did not come with any superiority of speech or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the mystery{a} of God.
For I made up my mind to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
And I came among you in weakness and fear and much trembling,
and my speech and my proclamation were not in persuasive words of wisdom,{b} but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
so that your faith would rest not on human wisdom but on God’s power.
Yet among the mature we do speak wisdom, though not a wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away.
Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom that God foreordained before the ages for our glory.
This wisdom not one of the rulers of this age has grasped; had they grasped it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.
But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not arisen in any human heart, all that God has made ready for those who love him”{c}
for it is to us that God has revealed them{d} through the Spirit. The Spirit searches out everything, even the depths of God.
For who among human beings knows what is in a person except that person’s own spirit within? In the same way no one comprehends what is in God except the Spirit of God.
Now we have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit that comes from God, so that we may know the things freely given us by God.
And we speak of these things in words taught not by human wisdom but by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people.{e}
The natural person{f} does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are discerned spiritually.
But the spiritual person discerns all things, and is himself discerned by no one.
For “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?”{g} But we have the mind of Christ.

notes.text: Mystery: so the Westcott–Hort text with P46 (probably), Sinaiticus (original hand), Alexandrinus, and Ephraemi (as reported); many manuscripts read “testimony.”
Persuasive words of wisdom: the manuscripts differ widely here; many read “persuasive words of human wisdom,” and P46 and a few others read “persuasion of wisdom” (as reported).
Isa 64:4 (64:3 Hebrew), freely; compare Isa 52:15; 65:17.

Revealed them: the sentence begun in v. 9 is incomplete in the Greek. “For” is the reading of the Westcott–Hort text, with P46 and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts read “but” (“But God has revealed them to us...”).
Interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people: or “combining spiritual things with spiritual words,” or “comparing spiritual things with spiritual.”
The natural person: Greek *psychikos anthrōpos*, the person who lives on the merely natural level, without the Spirit.
Isa 40:13, following the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.

verses.text: As for me, brothers, I was unable to talk to you as to people of the Spirit; I had to talk to you as to people of flesh, as to babies in Christ.
Milk was what I gave you to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Even now{a} you are still not able,
for you are still fleshly. As long as there is jealousy and strife among you,{b} are you not fleshly, behaving in merely human fashion?
When someone declares, “I am for Paul,” and someone else, “I am for Apollos,” is that not purely human?
Who is Apollos, then, and who is Paul? Just ministers by whose means you came to faith, as the Lord assigned to each.
I planted; Apollos watered; but it was God who kept making it grow.
So neither the planter nor the waterer counts for anything, but only God, who makes things grow.
The one who plants and the one who waters are one, and each will receive his own wages in keeping with his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.
In keeping with the grace God gave me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder would, and another is now building upon it. Let every builder watch how he builds.
For no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Whether a person builds on the foundation in gold or silver or costly stones, in wood or grass or straw,
each one’s work will become evident; for the Day will make it known, because it is revealed with fire, and the fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done.
If the work someone has built on it survives, he will receive a reward.
If the fire consumes someone’s work, he will bear the loss; yet he will be saved himself, though as one escaping through flames.
Do you not know that you are God’s temple{c} and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him. For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are.
Do not fool yourselves. Anyone among you who imagines himself wise by the standards of this age must become foolish in order to become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is folly in God’s sight. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their own craftiness,”{d}
and again, “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.”{e}
So let no one boast in human beings. For everything belongs to you,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future; all of it is yours,
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

notes.text: Even now: “even” translates *eti*, bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Among you: many later manuscripts add “and divisions.”
Temple: Greek *naos*, the sanctuary itself, where God dwells.
Ps 94:11 (93:11 Greek), following the Greek Old Testament, which reads “of human beings” where Paul has “of the wise.” In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.

verses.text: This is how one should regard us: as assistants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Moreover, what is required of stewards is that each be found trustworthy.
For my part, being put on trial by you, or by any human court,{a} matters very little to me; I do not even sit in judgment on myself.
For I am not aware of anything against myself, but that does not acquit me. The one who examines me is the Lord.

So do not pronounce judgment on anything before the appointed time, before the Lord comes, who will both bring to light what is hidden in darkness and lay bare the purposes of hearts. Then each one will receive his praise from God.

Brothers, I have used myself and Apollos to illustrate these points for your benefit, so that by our example you may learn the rule “Nothing beyond what stands written,” and none of you may swell with pride, siding with one man against another.
Who sets you apart as special? What do you possess that was not given to you? And if it was given, why boast as if it were your own achievement?
Already you are satisfied! Already you have become rich! You have begun to reign without us! I only wish you did reign, so that we too might reign with you.
I think God has exhibited us apostles at the tail end of the procession, like men sentenced to death, for we have been made a public show before the world, both angels and humans.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are sensible in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disgrace.
Up to this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed and knocked about, and we have no home of our own.
We wear ourselves out with the work of our own hands. When we are reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;
when slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the scum of the world, the dregs of everything, to this day.
I am not writing these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my dear children.
For though you may have countless guardians{b} in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
I urge you, then, be imitators of me.
That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus,{c} just as I teach them everywhere in every church.
Some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and then I will find out not the talk of these puffed-up people but their power.
God’s kingdom is a matter not of words but of power.
Which do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?

notes.text: Human court: literally “human day,” in contrast with the Day of the Lord.
Guardians: Greek *paidagōgos*, the household slave who supervised a child’s conduct and escorted him to school (compare Gal 3:24).
Jesus: bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.

verses.text: It is actually being reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and immorality of a kind not found even among the pagans: a man is living with his father’s wife.{a}
And you are puffed up! Should you not instead have gone into mourning, so that the man who did this would be removed from your company?
For my part, though absent in body, I am present in spirit, and as one present I have already passed judgment on the man who has done such a thing.
When you are assembled in the name of [our] Lord Jesus, and my spirit is with you along with the power of our Lord Jesus,
deliver such a man to Satan, for the ruin of his flesh, with a view to the rescue of his spirit on the Lord’s day.{b}
Your boasting is no good thing. Are you unaware that a little yeast leavens the whole lump of dough?
Clean out the old yeast, so that you may be a fresh batch, as in fact you are unleavened. For our Passover lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.{c}
So let us keep the festival not with old yeast, the yeast of vice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
In my letter{d} I wrote to you not to mix with sexually immoral people,
not meaning the immoral people of this world in general, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters; for then you would have to leave the world altogether.

What I am now writing to you is that you must not keep company with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater, a slanderer, a drunkard, or a swindler; with such a person do not even share a meal.
For what business is it of mine to judge outsiders? Is it not those inside whom you are to judge?
Those outside, God judges. “Drive out the wicked person from among you.”{e}

notes.text: Father’s wife: evidently his stepmother. Compare Lev 18:8.
The Lord’s day: that is, the day of the Lord’s coming. Many manuscripts add “Jesus,” and some “our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Sacrificed: many later manuscripts add “for us.”
My letter: an earlier letter of Paul to Corinth that has not survived.
Deut 17:7 and similar passages (Deut 19:19; 22:21, 24; 24:7).

verses.text: When one of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints?
Or are you unaware that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unfit to try the most trivial cases?
Are you not aware that angels will come under our judgment? Then surely the affairs of this life will!
So if you have such everyday cases, do you seat as judges those who carry no standing in the church?
I say this to put you to shame. Is there really not one wise person among you who will be able to settle a dispute between one brother and another?
Yet here is a brother suing a brother, and in front of unbelievers at that!
In fact, to have lawsuits with one another at all already means a defeat for you. Why not rather put up with wrong? Why not rather let yourselves be cheated?
Instead you yourselves do wrong and cheat, and you do it to brothers!
Or are you unaware that the unrighteous will not inherit God’s kingdom? Do not be led astray: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor *malakoi* nor *arsenokoitai*,{a}
nor those who steal or grasp for more, nor those given to drink, abusive speech, or extortion, will have any share in God’s kingdom.
And this is what some of you were. But you were washed clean, you were made holy, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ{b} and by the Spirit of our God.
“I am free to do anything,”{c} you say; but not everything does any good. “I am free to do anything”; but I will not let anything master me.
“Meals for the belly, and the belly for meals,” and God will bring both to nothing. But the body exists not for immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.
Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
Or do you not know that the man who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, it says, “The two will become one flesh.”{d}
Whoever is joined to the Lord, however, is one spirit with him.
Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits lies outside the body, but the sexually immoral man sins against his own body.
Or are you unaware that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for a price was paid for you. Honor God, then, with your body.{e}

notes.text: *Malakoi* … *arsenokoitai*: two Greek terms left untranslated here because their exact sense is disputed. *Malakoi* means literally “soft ones” and in this context is usually taken to refer to the passive partner in male homosexual acts; *arsenokoitai* (“men who lie with males”), apparently drawn from the Greek of Lev 18:22 and 20:13, is usually taken to refer to the active partner, though some interpreters limit both terms to exploitative practices such as pederasty or prostitution.
The Lord Jesus Christ: “our” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text after “the Lord.”
I am free to do anything: the quotation marks here and in v. 13 reflect the common view that Paul is citing slogans used at Corinth.
Body: many later manuscripts add “and in your spirit, which are God’s.”

verses.text: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.”{a}
But because of the cases of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
Let the husband give his wife what is due to her, and likewise the wife to her husband.
The wife has no exclusive right over her own body, but the husband has; likewise the husband has no exclusive right over his own body, but the wife has.

Stop refusing each other, unless it is by consent and for a limited time, to have leisure for prayer,{b} and afterward resume your relations, so that Satan does not tempt you because you lack self-control.
I say this, though, as a concession, not as a command.
My wish is that all people were like me; but each has his particular gift from God, this one in one way and that one in another.
My advice to those without spouses and to widows is that they do well to stay single as I do.
But if they are not exercising self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn with desire.
To the married I give this charge, not I but the Lord: a wife is not to separate from her husband
(and if she has separated, she should either stay unmarried or make peace with her husband), and the husband is not to send his wife away.
To everyone else I speak for myself, not for the Lord. Suppose a brother has an unbelieving wife who agrees to go on living with him: he should not send her away.
And suppose a woman has an unbelieving husband who agrees to go on living with her: she should not send him away.

For the unbelieving husband has been made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy through the brother.{c} Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.
But if the unbelieving partner separates, let the separation take place. In such circumstances the brother or the sister is not bound. God has called you{d} to live in peace.
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Only, let each person lead the life the Lord has assigned to him, the life in which God has called him. This is the rule I lay down in all the churches.
Was someone already circumcised when he was called? Let him not try to undo his circumcision. Has someone been called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision counts for nothing and uncircumcision counts for nothing; what counts is keeping God’s commandments.
Each one should stay in the condition in which he was called.
Were you a slave when called? Do not let it trouble you. But if you are actually able to become free, make use of the opportunity instead.{e}
For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one who was free when called is Christ’s slave.
A price was paid for you; do not turn yourselves into slaves of men.
Each one, brothers, in whatever condition he was called, in that let him remain before God.
About virgins I have received no instruction from the Lord, but I offer my view as someone the Lord in his mercy has made reliable.
My view, then, in light of the present crisis, is that a person does well to stay just as he is.
Tied to a wife? Do not look for a release. Released from a wife? Do not look for a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have trouble in the flesh, and I would spare you that.
What I mean, brothers, is this: the time has been cut short. From now on let those who have wives be as though they had none,
and those who weep as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no possessions,
and those who make use of the world as though not making full use of it. For the present shape of this world is passing away.
I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is concerned about the Lord’s affairs, how to please the Lord.
whereas the married man has the world’s affairs on his mind and how he may please his wife,

and he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned about the Lord’s affairs, so as to be holy in both body and spirit; but the married woman is concerned about the affairs of the world, how to please her husband.{f}
I am saying this for your own benefit, not to throw a noose around you, but to promote what is fitting and to secure undistracted devotion to the Lord.
If anyone thinks he is not behaving properly toward his virgin,{g} if she is past her prime and it has to be, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning. Let them marry.
But whoever stands firm in his heart, being under no compulsion but having control over his own will, and has decided in his own heart to keep her as his virgin, will do well.
So then the one who marries his virgin does well, and the one who does not marry will do better.
A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies,{h} she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
But she is more blessed, as I see it, if she stays as she is; and I believe I also have God’s Spirit.

notes.text: It is good…: most interpreters take this as a quotation from the Corinthians’ letter, which Paul then qualifies.
Prayer: many later manuscripts read “to fasting and prayer.”
Through the brother: that is, through the believing husband. Many later manuscripts read “through her husband.”
Called you: many manuscripts read “called us.”
Make use of the opportunity instead: or “rather make use of your present condition.” The Greek says only “rather use,” and interpreters divide over whether the object is freedom or slavery.

And he is divided…: the text and punctuation of vv. 33–34 vary among manuscripts. The translation follows the Westcott–Hort text; other manuscripts read “and the wife and the virgin are divided: the unmarried woman is concerned…”
His virgin: probably his fiancée, though some take it as a father and his virgin daughter (so that “marries” in v. 38 would mean “gives in marriage”), or as a couple living in spiritual marriage.
Dies: literally “falls asleep.”
